Reductive amination is a chemical reaction in which a carbonyl compound (such as an aldehyde or ketone) is converted into an amine by reacting it with an amine or ammonia in the presence of a reducing agent. This process is widely used in organic synthesis to form carbon-nitrogen bonds, which are common in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and other fine chemicals.

The general reaction can be represented as follows:

\[ \text{R-CO-R'} + \text{R''-NH}_2 \xrightarrow[\text{Reduction agent}]{\text{Conditions}} \text{R-CH(NR'')-R'} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \]

Where:
- R-CO-R' represents the carbonyl compound (aldehyde or ketone).
- R''-NH2 represents the amine or ammonia.
- R-CH(NR'')-R' represents the resulting amine product.
- H2O is water, a byproduct of the reaction.

The reducing agent used can vary depending on the specific conditions and substrates involved. Common reducing agents include sodium cyanoborohydride (NaBH3CN), sodium triacetoxyborohydride (NaBH(OAc)3), and catalytic hydrogenation using a metal catalyst like palladium on carbon (Pd/C) with hydrogen gas.

This reaction is particularly useful for the synthesis of amines from readily available carbonyl compounds and is a key step in the production of many biologically active molecules.
